samples.text:
The bar chart shows the percentage of teenagers in one country which owned five kinds of digital devices in 2012 and 2024.

In 2012, games console was the most popular device, 70% of teenagers had one. Laptop was 52% and smartphone was 45%, so smartphone was only in the third place. Only 18% of teenagers owned a tablet and nobody had a smartwatch.

In 2024, the smartphone became the most popular device and it increased to 96%, so nearly all teenagers had one. The smartphone had the biggest increase of 51 percentage points. Laptop also rose to 71% and tablet increase from 18% to 44%. Smartwatch was 0% in 2012 but in 2024 it was 29%. The only device which went down was games console, it fell from 70% to 62%.

Overall, most of devices became more common between 2012 and 2024, especially the smartphone. However, the games console was less popular in 2024 than in 2012, although it was still owned by many teenagers.
samples.why: Figures accurate with one useful calculation · simple overview at the end · mechanical linking and listing · repetitive vocabulary · article, relative-pronoun, verb-form and punctuation errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares the proportion of 13 to 17-year-olds in a particular country who owned five different digital devices in 2012 and 2024.

Overall, ownership of most devices increased significantly over the period, with smartphones replacing games consoles as the most commonly owned device. Games consoles were the only device to become less common.

In 2012, games consoles were the most widely owned device among teenagers, at 70%, followed by laptops (52%) and smartphones (45%). By 2024, however, smartphone ownership had more than doubled to 96%, meaning that almost every teenagers had one. Laptop ownership also rose, but more gradually, reaching 71%, whereas the proportion owning a games console fell slightly to 62%. As a result, games consoles dropped to third position, behind both smartphones and laptops.

The two remaining devices were much less common, although both saw considerable growth. The percentage of teenagers with a tablet increased from 18% to 44%, more than doubling, while smartwatches, which were not owned by any teenagers in 2012, had been acquired by 29% of them by 2024.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying the change in the leading device · key features highlighted and grouped logically · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
The chart compares the percentage of teenagers aged 13 to 17 in one country who owned each of five digital devices in 2012 and 2024.

The most significant development was the rapid spread of smartphones, which went from being owned by fewer than half of teenagers to near-universal ownership, displacing games consoles as the most common device. Ownership of every other device also grew, with the sole exception of games consoles.

In 2012, games consoles led the way, owned by 70% of teenagers, ahead of laptops at 52% and smartphones at 45%. Twelve years later, smartphone ownership had surged by 51 percentage points to 96%, while laptops saw a more moderate rise to 71%. Games consoles, by contrast, became slightly less widespread, with ownership slipping to 62%, though they remained the third most common device.

Tablets and smartwatches were owned by comparatively few teenagers but recorded notable gains. The proportion with a tablet more than doubled, from under a fifth (18%) to 44%, while smartwatches, which none of the teenagers owned in 2012, had been taken up by 29% by 2024.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected around the rise of smartphones · clear overview · accurate figures and derived changes · cohesion managed well · precise, natural vocabulary · varied, error-free structures.
